metaTitle: Do Carpenter Ants Bite? Yes, and What to Do
metaDescription: Yes, carpenter ants can bite but cannot sting, and may spray formic acid into the wound. Covers first aid, identification and why the nest matters more.
h1: Do Carpenter Ants Bite? What It Feels Like, First Aid and the Nest Behind It
dek: Carpenter ants can bite and cannot sting. Here is what the university sources say about the pain, how to treat a bite, and why a nest in your wood matters more than the bite.
excerpt: Carpenter ants can bite and cannot sting. What the bite feels like, how to treat it, how to recognize the ant, and why the nest is the bigger concern.

quickAnswer.lead: **Yes, carpenter ants can bite, but they cannot sting.** The University of California's [carpenter ant guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/carpenter-ants/) says the bite can be painful and that the ant may spray formic acid into the wound, causing a burning feeling. A Maryland fact sheet describes only a small nip. Wash the bite, ice it, and look for the nest, which matters more than the bite.
bullets: Workers are 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, and winged reproductives reach up to 3/4 inch, according to Penn State Extension.
Carpenter ants do not eat wood: University of California IPM says they excavate it to make nests, often starting where wood is damaged by water or decay.
MedlinePlus advises washing a bite with soap and water, then icing it for 10 minutes on and 10 minutes off.
Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or mouth, throat tightness, weakness or turning blue.
Penn State says a colony usually does not produce winged queens and males until it is several years old and has about 2,000 to 3,000 workers.
Penn State says carpenter ants usually will not infest sound wood below 15 percent moisture content, so a nest often points to a damp-wood problem.

body.text: Do carpenter ants bite?
Yes, carpenter ants can bite, and they cannot sting. Two university extension fact sheets say so, although they describe the bite very differently, and a third does not mention biting at all.

head: Source
What it says about carpenter ant bites
rows: Cannot sting. Can bite painfully with the jaws and spray formic acid into the wound, causing a burning sensation.
Does not sting. At most gives a little nip with the jaws if handled.
Covers identification, nesting and control, but does not address biting.
body.caption: Summaries of the three extension fact sheets used for this guide. Penn State's is listed because it is silent on the question, not because it disagrees.

body.text: The gap between a painful bite and a little nip is real, and neither page explains it. Neither measures pain or says how often bites happen, so the fair summary is that a bite is possible and ranges from a nip to a painful burn. Maryland's wording does say when to expect one: the nip comes if the ant is handled. Carpenter ants are one of several biting ants, and [which common US ants bite, which sting and which do both](/blog/do-ants-bite) is set out species by species on its own page. For the wider picture of household ants, the [complete guide to ants in US homes](/learn/ants) is the place to start.
Do carpenter ants spray formic acid?

According to the University of California, yes: a carpenter ant can spray formic acid into the wound its jaws make, and the acid causes a burning sensation. That is a detail from one source. The Maryland and Penn State fact sheets do not mention the acid, and none of the pages gives an amount, how strong the burn is or how long it lasts. The acid explains why a bite can burn, but nothing in these sources sizes the risk.
What does a carpenter ant bite feel like, and is it dangerous?

The sources describe a range from a small nip to a painful bite with a burning sensation, and none of the three fact sheets treats a bite as a medical hazard. Beyond that the evidence is thin. The fact sheets do not say how long the pain lasts, how often a bite breaks the skin, or whether welts or swelling are typical, so anyone describing those details is going further than these university sources do. For insect bites and stings in general, [MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000033.htm) says symptoms depend on the type of bite or sting and may include pain, redness, swelling, itching and burning, and that in most cases they can be easily treated at home.

Carpenter ants cannot sting, and the stinging insects that [MedlinePlus lists among the most common causes of anaphylaxis](https://medlineplus.gov/anaphylaxis.html) are a different group. That does not rule out an allergic reaction to a bite in someone who is sensitive, so the emergency signs below apply to a carpenter ant bite as they would to any other insect bite.
How do you treat a carpenter ant bite?

Treat it like any minor insect bite: clean it, cool it and watch it. These steps follow [MedlinePlus's first-aid guidance for insect bites and stings](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000033.htm), which covers bites and stings in general and is not specific to carpenter ants.

items: Wash the bite thoroughly with soap and water.
Put ice wrapped in a washcloth on the bite for 10 minutes, then take it off for 10 minutes, and repeat.
If necessary, take an antihistamine or apply a cream that reduces itching, following the package directions.
Over the next several days, watch for signs of infection such as increasing redness, swelling or pain.

body.text: MedlinePlus also tells readers to scrape out a stinger, but that step does not apply here because carpenter ants do not sting. If the bite looks worse instead of better after a few days, or you are unsure what you are seeing, contact a healthcare provider or pharmacist.

body.title: Call 911 for these signs
body.text: MedlinePlus says to call 911 or the local emergency number if someone with a sting has trouble breathing, wheezing or shortness of breath, swelling anywhere on the face or in the mouth, throat tightness or difficulty swallowing, or is feeling weak or turning blue. Treat the same signs after a bite as an emergency.

That list is worded for stings. [MedlinePlus's anaphylaxis page](https://medlineplus.gov/anaphylaxis.html) is not limited to them: it lists symptoms across the skin, nose, mouth, throat, chest, heart, digestive tract and nervous system, including hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, throat tightness, wheezing, a weak pulse, vomiting and fainting. It says to call 911 if someone is having a serious allergic reaction and, if an auto-injector is available, to give the injection right away.
How can you tell a carpenter ant from other ants?

A carpenter ant worker is a dark ant 1/4 to 1/2 inch long with one narrow waist segment and an evenly rounded back when viewed from the side. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/carpenter-ants) gives the size range and describes workers as dark, shiny brown to black, and the [UC IPM guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/carpenter-ants/) names the single node at the waist and the smooth, evenly rounded thorax profile as the features to check.

body.caption: Features as described in the cited extension fact sheets.

body.text: Color varies by species and region. UC IPM describes the western black carpenter ant, *Camponotus modoc*, as uniformly black with dark red legs and *C. vicinus* as variable in color but usually red and black. It also lists a smaller species common in California, *C. clarithorax*, as yellow and black and from a little over 1/8 inch to just under 5/16 inch long. University of Maryland Extension's fact sheet pictures the black carpenter ant, *Camponotus pennsylvanicus*, and says the winged queens and males seen in spring or early summer, at up to 3/4 inch, are the largest ants in Maryland. Other dark ants turn up indoors too, so [a comparison of carpenter ants with little black, pavement and odorous house ants](/blog/black-ants) helps when your ant does not quite match.
Why is the nest a bigger problem than the bite?

A bite is one ant's reaction, and a nest is a colony living in your wood. UC IPM says carpenter ants do not consume wood the way termites do but excavate it to make their nests, and University of Maryland Extension agrees that they do not consume wood but use it for nesting. A colony does not appear overnight. UC IPM says colony growth is slow at first and that a colony reaches maturity and starts producing winged ants only after several years, and it says the ants can build nests containing several thousand ants. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/carpenter-ants) says a colony usually does not produce winged queens and males until it is several years old and has about 2,000 to 3,000 workers.

The nest in your house is often not the whole colony. UC IPM says the nests carpenter ants build indoors are typically satellites of a larger parent nest outside, in a live or dead tree, a woodpile or landscaping materials, and Penn State says the parent colony is often in a tree, log or waste wood within 100 yards of the house. The sawdust in one wall may be only one part of it.
How much damage do carpenter ants really do?

The sources disagree on how much structural damage a nest causes, and they agree on moisture. UC IPM says nests often begin where there is damage from water or wood decay, and that from there the ants can expand the nest into sound wood and compromise structural integrity. Maryland says a colony inside a structure is usually most important as a sign that there is or has been a water problem. Penn State goes furthest the other way: it says the expansion of a nest into a building's wooden timbers rarely causes structural damage, and that when the ants tunnel through sound structural timbers to reach a void on the other side, it has little effect on the timber's structural integrity.

Penn State also says carpenter ants usually will not infest wood that is sound and has a moisture content below 15 percent, and that they seldom tunnel into dry, sound wood but may excavate moist, rotting wood and other soft materials to make satellite nests. Read together, the pages suggest the more urgent job may be the leak, clogged gutter or decayed timber that let the colony in.
What signs does a nest leave?

The clearest sign is a pile of wood waste. Penn State describes piles of coarse, stringy wood particles, dead insect parts and other debris sifting from cracks in siding, behind moldings, in the basement and attic, and under porches. University of Maryland Extension says the coarse sawdust looks similar to pencil shavings and indicates that a nest is close by, and UC IPM calls the sawdust fibrous. UC IPM adds a faint rustling in walls, floors and woodwork as another sign. The galleries themselves help separate carpenter ants from termites:

body.text: The full side-by-side of swarmers, workers and damage is in [the flying ants versus termites comparison](/blog/flying-ants-vs-termites), and it is the page to use if your sawdust has pellets in it instead of fibers.
Where do carpenter ants nest in a house?

Indoors, in wood that is damp or was damp, often in places you cannot see. Penn State lists the common sites and says they are places where wood may be wet or damp from poor ventilation, a leaking roof, defective flashing, overflowing or leaking gutters and downspouts, condensation from water pipes, or leaking bathtubs, showers or appliances. UC IPM adds voids and insulation:

items: **Structural timbers.** Porch pillars and supporting timbers, sills, girders, joists and wall studs, per Penn State.
**Around openings.** Window and door casings, also on Penn State's list.
**Voids and insulation.** UC IPM lists wall voids, hollow doors and insulation, and Penn State adds the space under insulation between ceiling joists or wall studs.
**Outdoors.** Logs, stumps and hollow trees, per Penn State, and woodpiles, per UC IPM.

body.text: Carpenter ants are most active after sunset, according to UC IPM, which is why you may notice them at night. Winged ants add another clue. Penn State says approximately 200 to 400 winged ants develop in a colony in summer, stay in the nest through the winter and leave the following spring or early summer, and UC IPM places the mating flights in spring. Penn State adds that numerous winged ants at windows inside the house probably came from an indoor nest, and [what an indoor flying ant swarm means](/blog/flying-ants) covers the timing and next steps.
What should you do if you find carpenter ants?

Find the nest before you treat anything. University of Maryland Extension says the best control for a severe infestation is to locate the nest and, if it is accessible, have a pest control professional apply pesticide directly to it. It says granular carpenter ant baits are available to pest controllers when the nest cannot be located, and that homeowners have the option of ant bait in small, sealed plastic trays. UC IPM says any bait used should be a slow-acting formulation, so the foragers carry it back and share it with the rest of the colony, which is critical because only about 10 percent of the ants are out foraging at any one time.

items: **Follow the trail after dark.** UC IPM suggests watching ant activity and following the workers back to the nest, preferably after sunset. Penn State suggests checking the basement, attic, garage and building exterior from May through July between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.

**Fix the moisture.** UC IPM recommends eliminating earth-to-wood contact and correcting causes of decay such as clogged rain gutters and leaky pipes, and Penn State says to keep wooden parts of the house dry by repairing roofs, flashing, gutters and downspouts.

**Read the label before using any bait or dust.** UC IPM names dusts containing the borate disodium octaborate tetrahydrate, and desiccant dusts such as diatomaceous earth, as effective control products. It warns that desiccant dusts can cause serious lung irritation if inhaled, and it says silica gel dust and fipronil perimeter sprays can be applied only by a licensed applicator.

**Check you have the right insect.** Carpenter ants are not the only insects that tunnel in wood, and [a guide to carpenter bees](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-carpenter-bees-canada) covers one of the others.

body.text: For a fuller walkthrough of locating and treating a colony, see [this guide to finding and removing a carpenter ant nest](/blog/carpenter-ants-canada). When the nest is inside the walls, [how to get rid of ants in the house](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-house) explains why bait beats spray, and [a comparison of ant killer and bait products](/blog/best-ant-killer) shows what the options are.
When should you call a professional?

Call one when the infestation is severe, when the nest is inside the structure, or when you cannot find it. Penn State says a satellite colony is unlikely to be eliminated without one or more of the materials that professional pest management companies apply, and it describes an outside perimeter treatment that is available to those companies. Maryland likewise ties severe infestations, and nests that cannot be located, to treatment by a professional.

Ask for an inspection that includes moisture sources, since UC IPM, Maryland and Penn State all tie nests to damp or decayed wood. If you are bitten, the first-aid steps above cover a minor bite, and the emergency signs are the ones to act on.

faqs.question: Do carpenter ants sting?
faqs.answer: No. The University of California's IPM program says carpenter ants cannot sting, and University of Maryland Extension says they do not sting. What they can do is bite with their jaws. UC IPM adds that they may spray formic acid into the bite wound, which causes a burning sensation. Maryland describes the most a handled ant can do as a little nip.

faqs.question: Why do I see carpenter ants in my house at night?
faqs.answer: Because they are most active after sunset, according to UC IPM. Seeing them after dark is useful rather than only annoying, since UC IPM suggests watching their activity and following the trails to find the nest. Penn State suggests checking the basement, attic, garage and building exterior from May through July between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. It lists sills, girders, joists and wall studs among the common indoor nest sites and says these are places where the wood may be wet or damp, so check for moisture problems near where the trail leads.

faqs.question: How big are carpenter ants?
faqs.answer: Workers are 1/4 to 1/2 inch long according to UC IPM, Penn State Extension and University of Maryland Extension, and Penn State and Maryland say the winged reproductives reach up to 3/4 inch. Penn State describes the color as dark, shiny brown to black, while UC IPM notes that one California species, Camponotus vicinus, is usually red and black. UC IPM also lists a smaller species common in California, Camponotus clarithorax, at a little over 1/8 inch to just under 5/16 inch.

faqs.question: Do carpenter ants eat wood?
faqs.answer: No. UC IPM and University of Maryland Extension both say carpenter ants use wood for nesting and do not consume it, which sets them apart from termites. UC IPM says they feed on dead and living insects, nectar, fruit juices and the sugary honeydew that plant-sucking insects excrete. The damage comes from the galleries they carve.

faqs.question: Can carpenter ants destroy a house?
faqs.answer: The sources differ. Penn State says the expansion of a nest into a building's wooden timbers rarely causes structural damage. UC IPM says nests can expand from water-damaged or decayed wood into sound wood and compromise structural integrity, and University of Maryland Extension says a colony indoors is usually most important as a sign of a past or present water problem. If you find fibrous sawdust or hear rustling in a wall, have the wood and the moisture source inspected rather than waiting to see which source is right.

faqs.question: Is a carpenter ant bite an emergency?
faqs.answer: Usually not, going by the sources used here. The extension fact sheets describe a nip or a painful, burning bite, and MedlinePlus says most insect bites and stings can be easily treated at home. Wash it with soap and water and ice it, as MedlinePlus advises. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or mouth, throat tightness, weakness or turning blue. Contact a healthcare provider if the bite looks worse after a few days or you are unsure.
